title: Week 7 · Block 2 — Errors & debugging
text:
How to read a traceback 🔍
Traceback (most recent call last):
  File "fasta_report.py", line 14, in <module>
    gc = gc_content(seq)
  File "seq_functions.py", line 3, in gc_content
    return gc / len(sequence)
ZeroDivisionError: division by zero


Bottom line = what went wrong 🎯
Above it = where, and how you got there
Read from the bottom up

title: Week 7 · Block 2 — Errors & debugging
text:
The usual suspects



Error
Usually means




SyntaxError
Missing : ) or quote


IndentationError
Wrong number of spaces


NameError
Typo, or variable not defined yet


TypeError
Mixing text and numbers


KeyError
That key is not in the dictionary


IndexError
Position beyond the end of the list


FileNotFoundError
Wrong path — run pwd 📍

title: Week 7 · Block 2 — Errors & debugging

Debugging with print() 🖨️
for line in f:
    line = line.strip()
    print("DEBUG:", repr(line))    # what is REALLY in there?
    if line.startswith(">"):
        ...

repr() shows the invisible: 'ATGC\n' vs 'ATGC' 👀

Professional debuggers exist — but print() is what everyone actually uses first.

title: Week 3 · Block 2 — Strings are sequences
text:
Indexing: counting from 0 🔢
seq = "ATGCGC"
seq[0]    # 'A'  — the FIRST letter
seq[1]    # 'T'
seq[-1]   # 'C'  — the last one







Note


Biologists count bases from 1, Python counts from 0. This causes real bugs in real papers. 🐛




10–25 min. Mention the classic off-by-one error in genomic coordinates (BED vs GFF).

title: Week 3 · Block 2 — Strings are sequences
text:
Slicing ✂️
seq = "ATGCGCTAGC"
seq[0:3]    # 'ATG'  — from 0 up to (not including) 3
seq[3:]     # from 3 to the end
seq[:3]     # from the start to 3
seq[::-1]   # reversed!

seq[start:stop] — stop is not included 🙂

title: Week 3 · Block 2 — Strings are sequences
text:
Useful string methods
seq.upper()              # 'ATGC'
seq.lower()              # 'atgc'
seq.replace("T", "U")    # DNA → RNA!
seq.count("GC")
seq.find("ATG")          # position of the first ATG (-1 if absent)
seq.startswith(">")      # True / False — FASTA headers!

A method does not change the original — it returns a new string.

Important: seq.upper() alone does nothing unless you assign it. Show the mistake live.

title: Week 3 · Block 2 — Strings are sequences
text:
Building strings
name = "seq1"

range() and while

title: Week 6 · Block 2 — Functions

text:
You keep writing the same thing 🔁
gc1 = (seq1.count("G") + seq1.count("C")) / len(seq1)
gc2 = (seq2.count("G") + seq2.count("C")) / len(seq2)
gc3 = (seq3.count("G") + seq3.count("C")) / len(seq3)

Change the formula → change it in three places. Forget one → silent bug 🐛

title: Week 6 · Block 2 — Functions
text:
Defining a function
def gc_content(sequence):
    gc = sequence.count("G") + sequence.count("C")
    return gc / len(sequence)
print(gc_content("ATGCGC"))
print(gc_content(seq2))

title: Week 6 · Block 2 — Functions
text:
Anatomy of a function
def gc_content(sequence, as_percent=False):   # parameters
    gc = sequence.count("G") + sequence.count("C")
    result = gc / len(sequence)
    if as_percent:
        result = result * 100
    return result                              # gives the value back
gc_content("ATGC")                  # 0.5
gc_content("ATGC", as_percent=True) # 50.0

Default arguments are optional to teach — but students love them once they see them.

title: Week 6 · Block 2 — Functions
text:
return is not print ⚠️
def bad(seq):
    print(len(seq))      # shows it, gives nothing back

def good(seq):
    return len(seq)      # gives a value you can USE

total = good("ATGC") + good("GGC")   # works ✅
total = bad("ATGC") + bad("GGC")     # TypeError 🚫

This is THE function misconception. Show the TypeError live and read it together.

title: Week 10 · Block 2 — Your project
text:
What makes a good project 🌟


Yes ✅

You can explain every line 🗣️
Honest README
Commits across several weeks


No 🚫

Code you cannot explain

A copy of the class exercises

title: Week 10 · Block 2 — Your project

The oral exam 💬
15 minutes, in week 14. We will talk about your code:

Walk me through your tool 🚶

A conversation, not an interrogation. I want to hear what you learned. 💛

title: Week 10 · Block 2 — Your project

⏱️ 25 min · alone, then share in breakout rooms
Create PROJECT.md in your repo:

What will your tool do? (2–3 sentences)

Output — what will it print or save?

Then: share it with your room and give each other one question 🤔

45–70 min. The “smallest working version” question saves half the failing projects. Rooms of 3 work well here — more perspectives.

title: Week 11 · Block 2 — Review & build
text:

Common fixable issues:

Functions that print instead of return ⚠️
Everything in one long block — no functions yet 🧩
No error handling: missing file → crash 💥
Commits: one giant “final” instead of steps 📈


All four are on the grading list. All four take 10 minutes to fix. ⏱️

20–30 min. Replace with what you actually saw in block 1 — specific beats generic.

title: Week 9 · Block 1 — Modules
text:
Your own module 📦
Any .py file is a module you can import.
# in analyse.py
from seq_functions import gc_content, reverse_complement

print(gc_content("ATGCGC"))

import seq_functions               # whole module
seq_functions.gc_content("ATGC")   # then use the prefix

10–25 min. They already did this in week 7 — now explain why it worked (same folder).

title: Week 9 · Block 1 — Modules
text:
The __main__ trick 🎩
# seq_functions.py
def gc_content(seq):
    ...

if __name__ == "__main__":
    print("Testing:", gc_content("ATGC"))   # runs ONLY when executed directly

Import it → the test does not run. Run it → it does. 🪄

Without this, importing a file runs all its top-level prints — confusing and messy.

title: Week 9 · Block 1 — Modules
text:
The standard library 🏛️
Python ships with hundreds of ready modules:
import os        # files and folders
import sys       # the script itself, arguments
import random    # random numbers
import math      # sqrt, log, ...
from collections import Counter   # counting, done for you 🎁
Counter("ATGCGC")   # Counter({'G': 2, 'C': 2, 'A': 1, 'T': 1})

Show Counter after they wrote counting by hand for two weeks — the reaction is always good.

title: Week 9 · Block 1 — Modules
text:
Installing packages 📥
pip3 install biopython
from Bio.Seq import Seq

s = Seq("ATGCGC")
print(s.reverse_complement())   # someone already wrote your function 🙂

But: you now understand what it does inside. That is the difference. 🧠

25–35 min. Important framing: libraries are not cheating — but blind use is. Biopython install may fail on some laptops; keep it optional, not required for the exercise.

title: Week 9 · Block 1 — Modules
text:
Exercise 1: Split your code 🧩
⏱️ 15 min · your own screen · react ✅

Make sure scripts/seq_functions.py has your functions only
Create scripts/run_analysis.py that imports them
Add the if __name__ == "__main__": block to seq_functions.py
Run both files — does each behave as expected?

💡 Bonus: replace your own count_bases with Counter and compare results

35–50 min. Import errors here are almost always about which folder they run python from.

title: Week 9 · Block 1 — Modules
text:
Exercise 2: Explore a module 🔭
⏱️ 25 min · breakout rooms
Each room picks one module: random · math · os · Counter

Find out what it does — read the docs, try it out
Write 3 short examples in scripts/explore_<module>.py
Find one use for it in a biology context 🧬
Be ready to show your room’s findings in 3 minutes 🎤


50–75 min. Assign modules so each is taken. Bring rooms back and let each present briefly — students teaching students.

title: Week 4 · Block 1 — Lists
text:
Working with lists
sequences = ["ATGC", "GGCA", "TTAG"]

sequences[0]        # 'ATGC' — same indexing as strings!
sequences[-1]       # 'TTAG'
len(sequences)      # 3
sequences[0:2]      # ['ATGC', 'GGCA'] — slicing works too

Lists hold anything: numbers, strings, even other lists.

title: Week 4 · Block 1 — Lists
text:
Changing lists ✏️
sequences.append("CCGG")     # add at the end
sequences.insert(0, "AAAA")  # add at a position
sequences.remove("GGCA")     # remove by value
last = sequences.pop()       # remove and return the last one
sequences[0] = "TTTT"        # replace







Note


Strings cannot be changed, lists can. seq[0] = "G" → error 🚫

title: Week 4 · Block 1 — Lists
text:
Useful list tools
lengths = [120, 85, 300, 42]

sum(lengths)          # 547
max(lengths)          # 300
min(lengths)          # 42
sorted(lengths)       # [42, 85, 120, 300]
len(lengths)          # 4
sum(lengths) / len(lengths)   # average 🧮

title: Week 4 · Block 1 — Lists
section: From string to list and back
text:
From string to list and back
header = ">seq1 Homo sapiens BRCA1"
parts = header.split()        # ['>seq1', 'Homo', 'sapiens', 'BRCA1']
parts[1]                      # 'Homo'

"-".join(["ATG", "CGC"])      # 'ATG-CGC'
list("ATGC")                  # ['A', 'T', 'G', 'C']

split() is how you will parse every data file 📄

Show splitting a CSV line: "seq1,120,0.42".split(","). This is the bridge to real files.

title: Week 4 · Block 1 — Lists
text:
Exercise 1: Predict, then run 🔮
⏱️ 10 min · chat first
seqs = ["ATG", "GGC"]
seqs.append("TTA")
print(len(seqs))
print(seqs[1])
print(seqs[1][0])      # 🤔
print(sorted(seqs))

25–35 min. seqs[1][0] is the key idea: indexing a list, then indexing the string inside it.

title: Week 4 · Block 1 — Lists
text:
Exercise 2: Sequence statistics 📊
⏱️ 25 min · breakout rooms · switch after 10 min
Create scripts/seq_stats.py:
sequences = ["ATGCGC", "GGCATTAGC", "TTA", "ATGGGCCCTA"]

How many sequences are there?
Print the first and the last one
Add one more sequence of your own
Make a list of their lengths (by hand is fine — 5 values)
Print the longest, shortest and average length
Split this header and print the species: ">seq1 Homo sapiens BRCA1"

💡 Bonus: print the sequences sorted alphabetically

35–70 min. Point 4 by hand is intentional — next block’s loops will feel like a relief.

title: Week 13 · Block 1 — Python vs R
text:
Same task, two languages


Python 🐍
lengths = [120, 85, 300]

total = sum(lengths)
avg = total / len(lengths)

long = []
for x in lengths:
    if x > 100:
        long.append(x)

R 🇷
lengths <- c(120, 85, 300)

avg <- mean(lengths)



long <- lengths[lengths > 100]


10–25 min. Let them see it, don’t over-explain. R wins on tables, Python wins elsewhere.

title: Week 13 · Block 1 — Python vs R
text:
The real skill 🧠
What transfers between every language:

Breaking a problem into steps 🧩
Variables, loops, conditions, functions
Reading error messages 🔍
Version control 💾
Asking: does this result make sense? 🤨



You did not learn Python. You learned to program — in Python. 🎓


25–35 min. This is the closing message of the whole course. Say it warmly.

title: Week 13 · Block 1 — Python vs R
text:
Exercise: Translate it 🔄
⏱️ 30 min · breakout rooms
Take one of your own Python scripts from weeks 3–7 and rewrite a piece of it in R:

Pick something small — GC content, filtering, counting
Write the R version in scripts/translated.R
Run both — do they give the same answer? ✅

💡 Bonus: which part was hardest to translate, and why?

35–70 min. The comparison of their own code is far more convincing than my slides. Common trap: indexing from 1, and strsplit() returning a list.
